transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose I should start with work, because that's really where it all kind of came to a head, you know? I'm a supervisor in retail, have been for a good long while, and communication is just... well, it's the whole job. You have to keep the floor moving and keep everyone on the same page. But lately, I came in today because... well, it's my words. I'll be standing there in the morning huddle, just trying to explain the inventory numbers, you know, the stock counts that come in overnight, or maybe I'm trying to lay out the weekend schedule for the floor staff. 

And instead of just saying who is on register one and who is in the back, my words just start... jumping. I'll start talking about the delivery trucks, and then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, because Thursdays are when the big shipments come, but then my brain goes straight to the church grill—we had a barbecue there last summer, you see—and then I'm going on about my boss's tone of voice when he called me yesterday. And I look at my team, these people I supervise, and they just have these blank stares. People are looking at me like they absolutely cannot follow a single thing I'm saying. It's embarrassing, really, because I have a degree, I know how to run a store, but the words just pile up and spill out in all the wrong directions, and I can't seem to make them line up the way they used to, and it's just making everything at the store so much harder than it needs to be.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed yourself feeling unusually energetic, euphoric, or needing much less sleep than normal?

Energetic? Euphoric? Oh, no, no. I mean, I wish, right? But no, not at all. If anything, it’s... well, it’s just the regular grind. You have to understand, being on your feet all day in retail at my age—I'm 59 now—it really takes it out of you. By the time I get home, take my shoes off, and finally sit down in my recliner, I'm just absolutely drained. The physical toll of walking those aisles, checking the endcaps, making sure the promotional signage is right... it just empties the tank. So, energetic is definitely not the word I would use. 

And as for sleep... no, I definitely don't feel like I need less of it. I need every single minute I can get, honestly. My alarm goes off at 5:30 AM every morning, because I have to be at the store by 7:00 to do the drawer counts and check the safe before we unlock the front doors at 8:00, and let me tell you, when that alarm sounds, I am not jumping out of bed ready to take on the world. I’m usually just dragging myself to the coffee maker. I try to get my solid seven hours every night. Sometimes my wife—she likes to watch those true crime documentaries out in the living room, and the sound carries right down the hallway—so sometimes that keeps me tossing and turning a little longer than I'd like, maybe delays me falling asleep by a half hour or so. But I'm certainly not staying up all night feeling like I don't need to rest. I'm just... I'm just a normal amount of tired, I suppose. Just trying to keep up with the daily schedule, which is hard enough right now with my words getting all tangled up, without feeling like I'm running a marathon on top of it.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or having strong beliefs that others have told you aren't true?

Voices? Beliefs? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, the store is loud, you know? Retail is just a constant hum of noise. You've got the overhead music playing—they just updated the playlist last week, actually, added a lot of 80s pop which is fine, I suppose, but it gets repetitive when you're there for an eight-hour shift. Then there's the beep of the registers, the PA announcements, the sound of the pallet jacks rolling across the linoleum... it's a lot of noise. Sometimes, if I'm in the back room doing inventory, I might hear a thump and think someone dropped a box, but it's just the pipes, or the HVAC unit kicking on. Old building, you see. Built in the late 90s, I think. 

But voices that aren't there? No. I hear my staff, I hear the customers complaining about the return policy—which, by the way, is printed right on the receipt, clear as day, but no one ever reads it. They just come up to the counter and expect you to bend the rules because they lost the tags. But that's real life, that's real people talking. I don't hear anything that nobody else hears. 

And as for strong beliefs... well, I believe in doing a good job. I believe in showing up on time, which is why I'm there at 7:00 AM sharp every day. I believe the district manager doesn't really understand the foot traffic patterns in our location, because he keeps pushing these endcap displays that just block the main aisle during the afternoon rush. I've told him this, of course. I sent a very detailed email about it last Tuesday, outlining the bottleneck it creates near the seasonal aisle. But nobody's telling me that's not true, they just ignore it because corporate mandates the floor plan. It's frustrating, but it's just business. Nobody is telling me I'm making things up or believing crazy things. It's really just my words, Doctor. Just the way they get all jumbled up when I'm trying to explain the shift changes or the break schedules. That's the only thing that's really out of sorts. Everything else is just the normal chaos of running a retail floor.
Around the time your words started getting jumbled, did you notice any other physical changes, like weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of your face or body, or a sudden severe headache?

Physical changes? Weakness? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, my back aches, sure, but that's just from the concrete floors at the store. We have those anti-fatigue mats behind the registers, but they only do so much, you know? And as a supervisor, I'm not standing in one spot anyway, I'm walking from the stockroom to the front end, back and forth, all day long. So my legs get tired, maybe a little heavy by the end of the week, but not weak like you're talking about. And definitely no numbness. 

As for my face drooping... well, I shave every morning, right? I stand in front of the mirror at 5:45 AM, and I'd notice if one side of my face wasn't doing what it was supposed to. I use a safety razor, have for years, and you have to be careful, pull the skin taut, so I'm looking right at my reflection. Everything looks perfectly normal. Both sides match. No drooping at all. 

And a sudden, severe headache? No. I mean, I get a mild headache sometimes if the fluorescent lights in the store are flickering—there's this one fixture in aisle four that maintenance just cannot seem to fix properly, they've been out twice this month and it still hums and flickers—but it's just a regular, annoying little headache. Nothing sudden or severe. Nothing that makes me stop what I'm doing. It's really just the talking, Doctor. Just my brain not sending the right words to my mouth when I'm trying to run the morning huddle. The rest of my body is working exactly the same as it always has.
When you think back to when this word-jumbling first started, did it come on suddenly—like within a day or so—or has it been developing gradually over weeks or months?

Suddenly? Oh, no. No, it wasn't like a light switch flipping, nothing like waking up one morning and suddenly not being able to get my sentences out. It’s been much more of a... a slow creep, I guess you could say. If I really sit down and think about it, looking back at the store's promotional calendar, it’s been noticeable for about six months now. 

I can actually pinpoint it because six months ago, we were right in the middle of a massive seasonal transition. We were moving all the summer patio furniture and clearance items to the back wall to make room for the back-to-school pallets. It’s a huge undertaking, rearranging half the store overnight, and I was trying to explain the new planogram to my morning crew. I remember I was talking to Kevin—he’s one of my stock boys, good kid, hard worker, but you really have to spell things out for him step-by-step or he puts the wrong price tags on things—and my explanations just started coming out all jumbled. I knew exactly what I wanted him to do with the display bins, but the instructions were just getting completely tangled up on the way out of my mouth. 

And around that same time, I started doing these... these odd stops. Right out there on the sales floor. I’d be in the middle of directing a customer to the electronics department, or explaining the lunch break schedule to the cashiers, and I would just stop. Just freeze up, lose the thread entirely, and stand there in silence. The district manager even caught it once during a regional walk-through when I was trying to explain our inventory shrink numbers. I just stopped talking for a good ten or fifteen seconds, right by the register banks. He looked at me like I had two heads. 

So, yeah, it’s been a solid six months of these jumbled up explanations and weird pauses on the floor. I kept thinking it would just clear up once the back-to-school rush was over, you know, thinking it was just the stress of the reset, but then we went right into the Halloween sets, and then Thanksgiving, and it’s just stuck with me the whole time. It definitely didn't happen overnight, just sort of built up over the last half-year until it got to the point where I couldn't just brush it off as being tired anymore.

Besides the word-finding and speech issues, have you or your family noticed any changes in your memory, ability to plan and organize tasks, or your personality and behavior over these past six months?

Memory? No, my memory is sharp. I know all the SKUs for our top hundred items by heart, and I know exactly when the delivery trucks are scheduled to hit the loading dock down to the minute. But... behavior? Planning? I mean, I guess there have been some... quirks lately. It's hard to explain without you seeing the layout of the store, but, well, take the front end for example. We have these impulse-buy displays right before you hit the checkout lanes. Batteries, chapstick, mints, that sort of thing. It's crucial real estate for our profit margins, so keeping it tidy is important. 

But lately, sometimes on the sales floor, I catch myself pacing that same aisle. Just walking up and down, up and down. And I'll be straightening the same row of batteries over and over again. I'll pull the AA packs forward—we call it 'facing' or 'fronting' the merchandise in retail—and I'll make sure they're perfectly aligned, no gaps, completely flush with the edge of the shelf. But then I'll get to the end of the rack, turn around, and start facing that exact same row of batteries all over again, even though I just did it and they're already perfect. I don't even really realize I'm doing it until I've paced that five-foot section maybe four or five times. 

And then with the planning, with organizing the tasks for the shift... I have this metal clipboard. It's one of those heavy aluminum ones that opens up, where I keep the break schedules, the daily zone assignments, and the shrink reports. Usually, I'm handing out assignments the second the morning huddle ends. 'Kevin, you're on seasonal, Sarah, you're backing up the registers,' right? I like to keep things moving. But recently, I'll just find myself standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand. Just... standing there, staring at the clip or looking down at the paper, not saying a single word. And the associates are all just standing around in a semi-circle, waiting for me to tell them what to do. They'll be looking at me, waiting for their assignments so they can get out on the floor, and I'm just glued to the linoleum holding this clipboard. 

Eventually, someone will clear their throat or say, 'Hey, boss, where do you need me?' and it sort of snaps me out of it. But it’s definitely not my normal management style. I’ve always been very efficient

Have your family or coworkers mentioned any changes in your personality lately—like seeming less interested in things you used to care about, acting more impulsively or inappropriately, or being less concerned about how your actions affect others?

Personality? Impulsive? No, no, definitely not. If anything, I'm the exact opposite of impulsive. You can't be impulsive in retail management, Doctor. We have a corporate handbook that's... well, it's about three inches thick, sits in this giant white binder right next to the microwave in the breakroom, and I know it front to back. I have to. As a supervisor, I'm the one setting the example for the whole shift. So acting inappropriately? Out of the question. I mean, if I started acting up, throwing caution to the wind or doing things off the cuff, HR would have my badge before the end of the week. I'm very careful about how I conduct myself. Always professional. Always wearing the proper name tag, shirt tucked in, making sure my radio earpiece is in so I can hear the front-end calls. 

And as for not caring about things, or not caring about how I affect people... that's just not me at all. I care a lot. Probably too much, if you ask my wife. I care deeply about my team and how the store runs. Like I mentioned Kevin earlier? I know he struggles with the planograms, but I don't just write him up or get mad. I take the time—when my brain isn't freezing up on me, anyway—to walk him through it. 

And I always, always make sure my cashiers get their state-mandated fifteen-minute breaks. You know, some managers in our district, they'll push those breaks back if the checkout lines get too long. Like if we get a sudden rush because the local high school just let out and all the teenagers are flooding in for energy drinks and chips, some supervisors will just make the cashiers work right through it. But not me. I know how hard it is standing on those concrete floors all day, even with those mats I was telling you about. I'm very mindful of how my actions impact them. If I don't give them their break on time, they get exhausted, their scanning speed drops, they get cranky with the customers, and then our store's customer satisfaction scores tank on the receipt surveys. It's all connected, you see? 

So no, my personality hasn't changed one bit. I'm still the exact same dedicated supervisor I've always been. I still care just as much about getting the endcaps perfectly aligned for the Sunday ad circulars, and I still treat my crew with respect. It's really just... it's just the words getting stuck, and the pacing in the battery aisle, and the freezing up with the clipboard. But inside? I'm exactly the same guy. No impulsive behavior whatsoever.
When people speak to you, do you have any trouble understanding what they're saying, or is the problem only with getting your own words out?

Understand them? Oh, no, no, I understand people just fine. My hearing is perfect, and I comprehend exactly what everyone is asking me. If a customer comes up and asks about the return policy on opened electronics, or if the district manager is asking about our year-over-year sales comps, I know exactly what they are saying. There is absolutely no confusion on my end when the information is coming in. 

The problem... the real reason I finally decided I needed to come in and see someone about this... is entirely about getting my own words out. It is just so frustrating. I will be standing there, say, trying to explain the inventory numbers to the morning team, or trying to go over the weekend schedule because we always have call-outs on Saturdays and I need to make sure the coverage is solid. I have it all perfectly lined up in my head. But when I open my mouth, my words just start jumping all over the place. 

It is like... well, I will start off talking about the delivery trucks, because obviously the freight schedule dictates our labor hours. But then, before I even finish the thought about the trucks, I am suddenly talking about Thursdays. And from Thursdays, for some absolutely inexplicable reason, my brain just completely derails and I start talking out loud about the church grill. The church grill! We had a cookout a while back, sure, but it has absolutely nothing to do with the store's weekend schedule or the freight pallets. And then from the grill, I am suddenly going on and on about my boss's tone of voice on the last regional conference call. 

It just bounces from the trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss's tone, just jumping from track to track, and I can see it happening in real time. I look at the people I am talking to, the cashiers or the stock crew, and they are just staring at me. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow a single thing I am saying. Their eyes just sort of glaze over, or they tilt their heads,
Outside of work, have you or your wife noticed any new difficulties handling everyday tasks—like managing bills, using the phone, cooking, or driving—that weren't a problem for you before?

Bills and cooking? No, I mean, I can still physically cook just fine. I make a very good meatloaf on Tuesdays, always have, and driving is perfectly fine. I drive my sedan down the interstate to work every single morning without a scratch. But... well, you mentioned my wife, and things *have* definitely changed with what I handle outside of the house. 

She’s actually had to start covering a lot of the commitments I used to handle for us. Like dealing with the homeowners association, or talking to the mechanics at the garage, or going to the bank to handle the safe deposit box. I used to do all of that because, like I said, I’m a manager. I'm used to dealing with people, I know how to negotiate and communicate. But lately, she’s had to step in and do it all because... well, because people started getting really uncomfortable around me. Or just completely confused. Because of the talking thing, you know? I'll be trying to ask the mechanic about the brake pads, and suddenly my words do that jumping thing, and I'm talking about the grocery store layout and then the church grill, and the guy in the greasy overalls

...just stands there staring at me like I have two heads. He is holding a wrench, I am talking about the church grill, and the whole thing just gets so incredibly awkward. So yes, my wife has had to cover all those commitments I used to handle for us at home, because people just started getting too uncomfortable or confused around me. Doctor, you didn't ask a question just now. You just... well, you just sort of paused, and I kept talking because, like I said, the mechanic was just standing there with the wrench. But I realize you might have been trying to ask me something else about the house or the bills or the cooking. I'm sorry, I get going and it's hard to stop sometimes. Did you have another question about what I do around the house, or the driving? Because I can tell you all about the commute, if you want. It's a 20-minute drive, straight down I-95, and I always take the left lane because the right lane gets backed up with the exit for the mall... but anyway, what were you going to ask?
Does anyone in your family—parents, siblings, or children—have a history of early-onset dementia, memory problems, or ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease)?

No, no, nothing like that. My family history is actually pretty clean when it comes to those kinds of things. My parents both lived well into their eighties, and they were sharp as tacks right up until the end. My father, he was a stubborn man, worked at the post office for forty years, and he could remember every zip code in the county even when he was eighty-two. Never had any memory issues, no dementia, certainly no ALS. And my mother, she was the same way, always doing her crossword puzzles in pen—Sunday Times, mind you, not the easy ones. 

As for my siblings, I have an older brother and a younger sister, and they're both doing fine. My brother just retired down in Florida, plays golf three days a week, and my sister is still teaching middle school math, so her brain is definitely working just fine. And my own kids, well, they're grown now, but they're perfectly healthy. No, there's no history of anything like that in my family. We've always been pretty lucky in the health department, physically speaking. It's just... well, just this talking thing with me lately. But no, no early-onset dementia or Lou Gehrig's or anything like that anywhere in the family tree, I'm quite certain of that. I've done the genealogy, actually, traced us back to the 1800s, and it's mostly heart stuff on my mother's side, but no brain diseases.

I'm sorry, did you ask something just now? Have you or your wife noticed any new trouble finding your way around familiar places, like getting confused on your usual drive to work or losing your bearings inside the store?

No, no trouble like that. I mean, I drive that same route to the store every single day, and it's practically muscle memory at this point. I pull out of the driveway, take a right on Elm, a left at the light by the old gas station—the one they turned into that fancy coffee shop, you know the one?—and then it's a straight shot down the highway. I don't even have to think about it. And inside the store, well, I've been a supervisor there for going on fifteen years now. I know where every single item is, from the seasonal displays in the front to the overstock in the back warehouse. If you asked me where the size 10 work boots are, I could walk you there blindfolded. 

My wife hasn't said anything about me getting lost, either. We go to the same grocery store every Sunday morning, right after breakfast, and I always push the cart while she checks the list. I never get turned around in the aisles or anything. The only thing she complains about is that I spend too much time talking to the produce guy, Frank, because Frank and I both follow the same baseball team, and, well, you know how it is when you get to talking about the playoffs. But no, getting lost or confused about where I am? That hasn't happened. I know exactly where I'm going, whether it's the drive to work, walking around the store, or just navigating the neighborhood. It's just... well, it's just the other things, the thoughts and the talking, but my sense of direction is as good as it's ever been. Better than my wife's, actually, she's the one who always needs the GPS if we go anywhere new, even if it's just a few towns over. But me? No, I'm perfectly fine with all that.

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose I should start with work, because that's really where it all kind of came to a head, you know? I'll start talking about the delivery trucks, and then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, because Thursdays are when the big shipments come, but then my brain goes straight to the church grill—we had a barbecue there last summer, you see—and then I'm going on about my boss's tone of voice when he called me yesterday. And I look at my team, these people I supervise, and they just have these blank stares. People are looking at me like they absolutely cannot follow a single thing I'm saying. It's embarrassing, really, because I have a degree, I know how to run a store, but the words just pile up and spill out in all the wrong directions, and I can't seem to make them line up the way they used to, and it's just making everything at the store so much harder than it needs to be.

Never had any memory issues, no dementia, certainly no ALS. And my mother, she was the same way, always doing her crossword puzzles in pen—Sunday Times, mind you, not the easy ones.

My brother just retired down in Florida, plays golf three days a week, and my sister is still teaching middle school math, so her brain is definitely working just fine. And my own kids, well, they're grown now, but they're perfectly healthy. No, there's no history of anything like that in my family. But no, no early-onset dementia or Lou Gehrig's or anything like that anywhere in the family tree, I'm quite certain of that. No, no trouble like that. I mean, I drive that same route to the store every single day, and it's practically muscle memory at this point. I pull out of the driveway, take a right on Elm, a left at the light by the old gas station—the one they turned into that fancy coffee shop, you know the one?—and then it's a straight shot down the highway. I don't even have to think about it. And inside the store, well, I've been a supervisor there for going on fifteen years now. I know where every single item is, from the seasonal displays in the front to the overstock in the back warehouse. If you asked me where the size 10 work boots are, I could walk you there blindfolded. 

My wife hasn't said anything about me getting lost, either. We go to the same grocery store every Sunday morning, right after breakfast, and I always push the cart while she checks the list. I never get turned around in the aisles or anything. The only thing she complains about is that I spend too much time talking to the produce guy, Frank, because Frank and I both follow the same baseball team, and, well, you know how it is when you get to talking about the playoffs. But no, getting lost or confused about where I am? That hasn't happened. I know exactly where I'm going, whether it's the drive to work, walking around the store, or just navigating the neighborhood. It's just... well, it's just the other things, the thoughts and the talking, but my sense of direction is as good as it's ever been. Better than my wife's, actually, she's the one who always needs the GPS if we go anywhere new, even if it's just a few towns over. But me? No, I'm perfectly fine with all that.
